e.etymology: From the biblical place name Salem (Hebrew Shalem), the city of Melchizedek in Genesis, related to shalom, peace. As a boy's name it can also be Arabic Salim, safe and sound.

assoc.t: Salem, Massachusetts, site of the 1692 witch trials
Sabrina the Teenage Witch's talking black cat
capital of Oregon
Salem menthol cigarettes

e.note: Most Americans link Salem with the 1692 witch trials, which gives the name a witchy, Halloween feel.

e.etymology: An Irish name made famous by Brian Boru, the high king who died in 1014. It probably comes from an old Celtic word for a hill or for something high.
namesakes: Brian Griffin (the talking dog on Family Guy)

e.etymology: A spelling of Eliana, from Hebrew Eli'ana, my God has answered. Eliana is also an Italian, Spanish and Portuguese name that goes back to the Roman family name Aelianus.
From Haerviu, the name of a Breton saint, from Old Breton hoiarn, iron, and viu, blazing. Bretons who came over with the Normans brought it to England, where it also became a surname.
namesakes: Harvey Milk (San Francisco politician and gay rights pioneer)

assoc.t: hurricane that flooded Houston in 2017
Harvey Weinstein, film producer convicted of sex crimes
invisible rabbit of the 1950 James Stewart film

e.note: Some people still connect the name with disgraced film producer Harvey Weinstein.

e.meaning: of Mars, the Roman god of war
e.etymology: From Latin Martinus, a derivative of Mars, the god of war. It spread across Europe through Saint Martin of Tours, the 4th-century soldier who cut his cloak in half for a beggar.
namesakes: Martin Luther King Jr. (civil rights leader)
Martin Luther (leader of the Protestant Reformation)

assoc.t: Martin acoustic guitars
Martin, the 1990s sitcom starring Martin Lawrence

e.meaning: a banded gemstone, best known in black
e.etymology: From the English word for the gemstone, most familiar in its black form. The word comes from Greek onyx, claw or fingernail, after the pale bands in some stones.

assoc.t: onyx, the black gemstone
Onyx, 1990s hip-hop group known for Slam

e.etymology: From Italian Giulietta, a pet form of Giulia, the Italian Julia, which comes from the Roman family name Julius. Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet fixed the English spelling.

assoc.t: Shakespeare's heroine in Romeo and Juliet

e.etymology: A surname meaning son of Ander, a medieval form of Andrew, common in Scotland after its patron saint. In the US it also absorbed Scandinavian Andersen and Andersson.

e.meaning: victory of the people; also young pup
e.etymology: Two names in one: a medieval pet form of Col, short for Nicholas, and an English form of Scottish Gaelic Cailean and Irish Coileán, young pup.
namesakes: Colin Powell (general and US secretary of state)

e.etymology: From Spanish cruz, cross, a religious name honoring the cross of Christ and long given to both boys and girls in Spanish. It is also a very common Hispanic surname.

assoc.t: Texas senator Ted Cruz
Cruz Ramirez, the yellow racer in Pixar's Cars 3

e.etymology: From an English surname taken from several places called Leighton, Old English leac, leek or herb, plus tun, farm or settlement.

e.meaning: hope, trust in a good outcome
e.etymology: From the English word, one of the three Christian virtues with Faith and Charity. Puritans began giving it as a name in the 1600s.
A spelling of Emery, a surname from a Norman personal name of Germanic origin whose second part means ruler. Emory University in Atlanta has kept this spelling familiar.

assoc.t: Emory University in Atlanta

e.etymology: From an English surname for someone from a small place in Sussex, named from the Old English personal name Paega plus tun, settlement.

assoc.t: Chicago Bears running back Walter Payton

e.etymology: An Italian name from Late Greek Rhomaios, Roman, used in the Middle Ages for someone who had made a pilgrimage to Rome. Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet carried it around the world.
namesakes: Romeo Miller (rapper and actor known as Lil' Romeo)

assoc.t: Shakespeare's young lover in Romeo and Juliet
a Romeo: a flirt or ladies' man

e.note: Calling someone a Romeo means a flirt or ladies' man, and Juliet jokes are likely.

e.etymology: From the English occupational surname for a baker or the keeper of a communal oven. Its use as a first name is recent and follows Carter, Cooper and Sawyer.

assoc.t: baker, a person who bakes bread and pastries
Baker's baking chocolate

e.etymology: A medieval Italian short form of Durante, from Latin durans, enduring. The poet Dante Alighieri, author of the Divine Comedy, made it famous.

assoc.t: Dante Alighieri, poet of the Inferno
demon hunter of the Devil May Cry video games

e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who lived beside a brook. It grew popular for girls in the 1970s and 1980s, helped by the actress Brooke Shields.

e.meaning: Hawaiian form of Mary; also calm
e.etymology: The Hawaiian form of Maria, the biblical Mary. Some bearers take it instead from the Hawaiian word malia, calm.
namesakes: Malia Obama (elder daughter of Barack and Michelle Obama)

assoc.t: Malia Obama, elder daughter of Barack Obama

e.meaning: a pause to reflect (a word from the Psalms)
e.etymology: A Hebrew word that closes many verses in the Psalms, thought to mark a musical pause or a moment to reflect; its exact sense is unknown. It became a girls' name in the 2000s.

assoc.t: Selah, a contemporary Christian vocal group

e.etymology: From the English word, which comes from Old French journee, a day's travel. American parents began using it as a name in the 1990s.

assoc.t: Journey, rock band behind Don't Stop Believin'
Journeys, mall shoe store chain

e.etymology: A Scottish pet form of Margaret, built on Mairead, the Gaelic form of the name, with the ending -sie. Margaret comes from Greek margarites, pearl.
namesakes: Maisie Williams (actress, Arya Stark in Game of Thrones)

e.etymology: A pet form of Scott, a surname and first name that first meant a person from Scotland or a Gaelic speaker. Long a boys' nickname, it has become mostly a girls' name in the US in recent years.
namesakes: Scottie Pippen (Chicago Bulls Hall of Famer)

assoc.t: Scottie, the Scottish terrier dog breed
Scottie Pippen, Bulls star, and golfer Scottie Scheffler

e.etymology: The French form of Damian, from the Greek name Damianos, linked to damao, to tame. Saints Cosmas and Damian, early Christian physicians, spread the name.
namesakes: Damien Chazelle (director of La La Land)
Father Damien (saint who cared for leprosy patients on Molokai)

assoc.t: Damien, the Antichrist child in The Omen

e.note: Some still think of Damien, the devil child of the 1976 horror film The Omen.

e.meaning: the victorious (from the city's Arabic name)
e.etymology: Taken from the capital of Egypt, whose Arabic name al-Qahira means the victorious. It has been used as an American given name mainly since the 2010s.

assoc.t: capital of Egypt, on the Nile

e.etymology: A pet form of Margaret, from Greek margarites, pearl. It has been used as a name in its own right since the 1800s.
namesakes: Maggie Smith (actress, Harry Potter and Downton Abbey)
Maggie Simpson (the baby on The Simpsons)

assoc.t: Maggie, the baby on The Simpsons

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Aubrey, the Norman French form of the Germanic name Alberich, from words for elf and ruler. Aubrey was mostly a man's name until the late 20th century.
The English word, from Latin sanctus, holy. Its use as a first name took off after Kim Kardashian and Kanye West named their son Saint in 2015.
namesakes: Saint West (son of Kim Kardashian and Kanye West)

assoc.t: Saint West, son of Kim Kardashian and Kanye West

e.etymology: A spelling of Alaina, a feminine form of Alan and its French form Alain, a Breton name whose meaning is uncertain.
The French and Portuguese form of Andrew, André, from Greek Andreas, built on aner, man. Americans usually write it without the accent.
namesakes: Andre the Giant (wrestler and actor in The Princess Bride)

assoc.t: Andre the Giant, wrestler and Princess Bride actor
André, a budget sparkling wine

e.etymology: From a surname: in Scotland a form of Stirling, the town, and in England sometimes a form of Starling. Most people hear the English word sterling, of high quality, as in sterling silver.
namesakes: Sterling K. Brown (actor, This Is Us)
Sterling Archer (spy in the animated series Archer)

assoc.t: sterling silver and the British pound sterling

e.etymology: From the Irish surname O Suilleabhain, descendant of Suilleabhan, a byname built on suil, eye, and usually read as little dark-eyed one.

assoc.t: Ed Sullivan, host of the classic TV variety show
Sulley (James P. Sullivan) of Monsters, Inc.
